newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Semis - Over the budget hurdles.
newsitem.headline: Australian Semis - Over the budget hurdles.

text.p: TCV NSW T-CORP QTC
SAFA WATC TASCOR
*Semi-government bonds' recent bid tone remains reasonably solid with the batch of state budgets providing few negatives and S&P providing a clean bill of health.

The strong bid tone seen for semi-government bond issues in recent weeks remains reasonably solid, and there were few negatives seen in the recent batch of state budgets to cause concern, analysts said on Monday,

Indeed, Standard & Poor's gave the states a clean bill of health in its monthly CreditFocus publication saying the debt burdens of Australian states should decline further in fiscal 1997, auguring well for their ratings in the medium term.

"The Australian states consolidated their rating positions in fiscal 1996 with very strong financial performances and continue to demonstrate sound financial fundamentals into fiscal 1997," the credit rating agency said.

The market's main driving force has been the possibility of the Reserve Bank changing its prudential supervision arrangements and New South Wales state considering the sell-off of its A$22 million power industry.
The latter would effectively wipe out NSW's debt, while the former could see state bonds included in banks' prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements, reducing already falling semis supply.
Highlighting the current demand for semis was an extremely tightly bid bond tender on Monday for Treasury Corp of Victoria, which saw A$100 million of its 2008 stock up for grabs.
The bonds fetched a weighted average yield of 7.6673 percent with bids in a 7.665 to 7.670 percent range.

Last week's Queensland 1997/98 budget projected a A$13.6 million underlying surplus compared with an estimated A$10.9 million in 1996/97, although a one-off surge in capital spending will see a A$99 million headline deficit.
Commonwealth Bank analyst David Thurtell noted Queenland's government debt to Commonwealth government securities (CGS) has narrowed in the past year and he expects them to remain relatively narrow.

"The spread of Queensland semis to CGS is expected to remain tight over the coming year, reflecting the strong growth prospects for Queensland and the robust fiscal position of the Queensland government," Thurtell said.
The Queensland government is forecasting 4.5 percent growth in 1997/98 following a 4.0 percent rise in 1996/97.
South Australia also handed down its 1997/98 budget, which projected an underlying A$1 million surplus compared with a A$59 million underlying deficit for 1996/97.
This would be the state's first surplus since World War Two, noted Andrew Gill, economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
"South Australia's fiscal position has improved considerably since the early 1990's and this budget continues with this trend," Gill said.
"This budget in no way threatens South Australia's fiscal position. Indeed, the gradual reductions in state debt further bolster South Australia's fiscal position," Gill added.
